categories.name: AI Safety & Ethics
categories.description: Align, evaluate, and secure AI systems against risks and harms.

questions.prompt: What does supervised learning use to train a model?

options.text: Labeled examples
Only unlabeled examples
Random outputs alone
A fixed set of rules

questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns from examples paired with target labels.
questions.learnNote: Training datasets can contain examples paired with expected outputs.

questions.prompt: What is overfitting?

options.text: Performing well on training data but poorly on unseen data
Performing equally well on all datasets
Having too little training data stored
Using a model only once

questions.explanation: An overfit model captures training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
questions.learnNote: Compare performance on the training set with held-out data.

questions.prompt: What is a feature in machine learning?

options.text: An input variable used by a model
The final model score
A server deployment
A training error message

questions.explanation: Features are input attributes used to make predictions.
questions.learnNote: Models use measurable properties of an example as inputs.

questions.prompt: Why reserve a test dataset?

options.text: To estimate performance on unseen examples
To train the model repeatedly
To store model weights
To guarantee zero errors

questions.explanation: A held-out test set provides an estimate of generalization.
questions.learnNote: Reliable evaluation needs data that did not guide model fitting.

questions.prompt: What does classification predict?

options.text: A discrete category
Only a continuous number
A database schema
A network address

questions.explanation: Classification assigns an example to a class or category.
questions.learnNote: Common prediction tasks distinguish categories from numeric quantities.

questions.prompt: What is inference?

options.text: Using a trained model to generate a prediction
Labeling all training examples
Deleting a training set
Changing model architecture only

questions.explanation: Inference applies a trained model to new input.
questions.learnNote: A model has a training phase and a separate usage phase.

questions.prompt: What does a high false positive rate indicate?

options.text: Many negative cases are incorrectly marked positive
Many positive cases are correctly detected
All labels are correct
The dataset has no negative cases

questions.explanation: A false positive is a negative example predicted as positive.
questions.learnNote: Consider errors made when predicting the positive class.

questions.prompt: What is a model parameter?

options.text: A learned numerical value used by the model
A user interface color
A test dataset label only
A deployment URL

questions.explanation: Parameters are values adjusted during training that affect model behavior.
questions.learnNote: Training adjusts numerical values inside a model.

questions.prompt: What does data leakage cause?

options.text: An overly optimistic evaluation from unavailable information
An encrypted training set
A smaller model file
A guaranteed fair model

questions.explanation: Leakage allows information unavailable at prediction time to influence training or evaluation.
questions.learnNote: Separate information available at prediction time from future or test-set information.

questions.prompt: What is a common goal of regularization?

options.text: Improve generalization by constraining model complexity
Guarantee perfect training accuracy
Remove the need for validation
Replace all training examples

questions.explanation: Regularization discourages overly complex solutions that may overfit.
questions.learnNote: Generalization can improve when model complexity is controlled.

questions.prompt: What is unsupervised learning primarily used for?

options.text: Discovering patterns or groupings in unlabeled data
Training models with explicit ground truth labels
Directly minimizing test set classification loss
Deploying model weights to edge devices

questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds underlying structure, patterns, or clusters without target labels.
questions.learnNote: Some learning tasks do not require explicit target outputs for training.

questions.prompt: What does underfitting indicate about a machine learning model?

options.text: The model is too simple to capture the underlying structure of the data
The model memorized the training set with zero error
The test dataset is larger than the training dataset
The model has too many parameters relative to dataset size

questions.explanation: Underfitting occurs when a model lacks the capacity or complexity to learn patterns from the training data.
questions.learnNote: Consider whether a model has sufficient expressive capacity for the problem.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a loss function during model training?

options.text: Quantifying the difference between predicted outputs and ground truth
Compressing model weights for faster deployment
Formatting user input into model tokens
Measuring the network latency of inference endpoints

questions.explanation: Loss functions measure error between predictions and true targets, guiding optimization.
questions.learnNote: Optimization algorithms require a numeric measure of prediction error to guide parameter updates.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between precision and recall?

options.text: Precision measures correctness among positive predictions; recall measures coverage of actual positives
Precision measures latency; recall measures throughput
Precision applies only to regression; recall applies only to classification
Precision evaluates training data; recall evaluates test data

questions.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives, while recall is true positives divided by all actual positives.
questions.learnNote: Evaluating classifier errors involves balancing false alarms against missed detections.

questions.prompt: Why is data normalization or feature scaling commonly applied before training?

options.text: To bring features onto comparable scales and stabilize optimization
To convert all categorical values into binary labels
To remove the need for a separate validation split
To encrypt features against unauthorized access

questions.explanation: Scaling features to similar ranges prevents features with large numeric values from dominating gradients.
questions.learnNote: Optimization algorithms often converge faster when inputs share similar numeric ranges.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the validation dataset during model development?

options.text: Tuning hyperparameters and selecting the best model checkpoint before final testing
Directly updating gradient weights during backpropagation
Encrypting the training pipeline against data tampering
Serving as production traffic for deployed services

questions.explanation: Validation data guides hyperparameter tuning and model selection without contaminating the held-out test set.
questions.learnNote: Models need a separate dataset to guide design choices without testing on the final evaluation set.

questions.prompt: What is backpropagation in neural network training?

options.text: Computing gradients of the loss function with respect to weights using the chain rule
Reversing the order of training examples in each epoch
Converting continuous predictions into discrete classifications
Deploying model weights backwards through a network cluster

questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus to calculate gradients layer-by-layer backwards from the loss.
questions.learnNote: Training neural networks involves determining how each internal weight contributes to the final error.

questions.prompt: What does the bias-variance tradeoff describe?

options.text: The tension between underfitting from oversimplified assumptions and overfitting from excessive sensitivity to training data
The balance between training speed and inference memory consumption
The difference between labeled and unlabeled training examples
The tradeoff between CPU and GPU hardware utilization

questions.explanation: High bias causes underfitting by missing relevant relations; high variance causes overfitting by modeling random noise.
questions.learnNote: Model error can stem from being too rigid or from being overly sensitive to training variations.

questions.prompt: What is transfer learning?

options.text: Reusing a model pretrained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task
Migrating a database from one cloud provider to another
Converting Python model code into client-side JavaScript
Shuffling training batches between different GPU devices

questions.explanation: Transfer learning leverages knowledge learned from large datasets to achieve strong performance on new tasks with less data.
questions.learnNote: Representations learned on broad datasets can be adapted for specialized downstream tasks.

questions.prompt: What is data augmentation?

options.text: Creating synthetic variations of existing training examples to improve generalization
Replacing all original training data with random noise
Encrypting database records to prevent unauthorized access
Compressing model weights to reduce memory usage

questions.explanation: Data augmentation applies transformations to increase dataset diversity and prevent overfitting.
questions.learnNote: Generating realistic variations of existing training data can help models generalize better.

questions.prompt: What is a token in an LLM?

options.text: A unit of text processed by the model
A guaranteed whole word
A database password
A GPU device

questions.explanation: Tokens are units of text that can represent words, parts of words, or other text.
questions.learnNote: Text is split into units that are not always whole words.

questions.prompt: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?

options.text: Adding retrieved context to a model request
Retraining a model after every question
Removing context from a prompt
Storing only generated answers

questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant information and supplies it as context for generation.
questions.learnNote: External documents can provide context at request time.

questions.prompt: What is a context window?

options.text: The amount of input and output a model can process together
A browser pop-up
The time required to train a model
A permanent database

questions.explanation: The context window limits the tokens considered in a model interaction.
questions.learnNote: Model interactions have a finite capacity measured in tokens.

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination?

options.text: A plausible but unsupported or false model output
A guaranteed citation
An input validation rule
An encryption method

questions.explanation: A model can generate fluent content that is incorrect or unsupported.
questions.learnNote: Fluent output is not necessarily factual.

questions.prompt: Why validate structured model output?

options.text: Generated output can violate the expected schema
Models always return valid JSON
Validation increases context size
It replaces access control

questions.explanation: Schema validation catches malformed or unexpected generated data.
questions.learnNote: A downstream application may require specific fields and types.

questions.prompt: What is prompt injection?

options.text: Untrusted content attempting to override application instructions
A method to compress model weights
A type of GPU
A deterministic search algorithm

questions.explanation: Prompt injection uses untrusted text to redirect model behavior.
questions.learnNote: Retrieved pages and user content can contain adversarial instructions.

questions.prompt: What is an embedding commonly used for?

options.text: Representing content as vectors for similarity search
Guaranteeing factual generation
Replacing authorization
Storing plaintext passwords

questions.explanation: Embeddings map content to numerical vectors useful for similarity comparisons.
questions.learnNote: Semantic search can compare numerical representations of content.

questions.prompt: What does temperature generally influence?

options.text: The randomness of generated outputs
The number of model parameters
The server clock
The size of the training dataset

questions.explanation: Temperature changes the sampling distribution and thus output variability.
questions.learnNote: Generation settings can influence how varied sampled outputs are.

questions.prompt: Why use a representative evaluation set?

options.text: To measure behavior on realistic tasks and edge cases
To guarantee a model never fails
To remove the need for monitoring
To hide poor results

questions.explanation: Representative evaluations reveal performance across tasks the application actually faces.
questions.learnNote: An evaluation should resemble the situations the application will encounter.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a system instruction?

options.text: To provide higher-level behavioral guidance to the model
To guarantee that all untrusted text is safe
To store embeddings permanently
To encrypt user messages

questions.explanation: System instructions guide behavior but do not eliminate the need for security controls.
questions.learnNote: Applications can supply instructions at different levels of authority.

questions.prompt: What is few-shot prompting?

options.text: Providing example input-output pairs within the prompt to guide model responses
Fine-tuning model weights with a small number of training steps
Prompting a model with fewer than ten tokens
Querying multiple models in parallel and selecting the fastest output

questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting conditions the model on demonstrations in the prompt without modifying weights.
questions.learnNote: Demonstrations provided in the prompt context can illustrate the desired formatting and reasoning.

questions.prompt: What problem does chunking address in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Splitting large documents into semantically coherent segments that fit context limits
Translating human text into programming language syntax
Encrypting stored embeddings in the vector index
Replacing semantic search with keyword indexing

questions.explanation: Chunking divides source documents into manageable passages suitable for retrieval and embedding within context constraints.
questions.learnNote: Long source documents often exceed optimal retrieval and context window boundaries.

questions.prompt: What does fine-tuning an LLM involve compared to prompting?

options.text: Updating model weights on task-specific training data
Adding retrieval context to the prompt at inference time
Changing only the temperature setting on API calls
Replacing the model tokenizer with a parser

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning modifies the model's learned weights, whereas prompting adapts behavior entirely in-context.
questions.learnNote: Adapting an LLM can be done at inference time via context or ahead of time by adjusting parameters.

questions.prompt: What is semantic caching in an LLM application?

options.text: Reusing stored responses for queries with equivalent meaning based on embedding similarity
Caching static web assets on a content delivery network
Storing prompt templates in local browser storage
Saving database transaction logs to disk

questions.explanation: Semantic caching matches incoming prompts by meaning rather than exact string equality to save cost and latency.
questions.learnNote: Users often ask questions with different wording that share the same underlying intent.

questions.prompt: What is chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting?

options.text: Encouraging the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer
Connecting multiple external databases into a single query pipeline
Chaining together sequential API calls without parsing intermediate results
Executing user code directly in the model environment

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting prompts the model to break complex reasoning into explicit sequential steps.
questions.learnNote: Prompting models to show step-by-step thinking can improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a re-ranker in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Scoring and reordering retrieved candidate passages to prioritize the most relevant context
Splitting source documents into tokenized sentences
Compressing vector embeddings for storage in memory
Generating final user-facing responses directly

questions.explanation: A re-ranker uses a more accurate cross-encoder model to score the top retrieval candidates before injecting them into the prompt.
questions.learnNote: Initial retrieval can retrieve multiple candidates that benefit from finer relevance scoring.

questions.prompt: What is jailbreaking in the context of LLMs?

options.text: Crafting prompts specifically designed to bypass model safety filters and guardrails
Rooting the operating system of a GPU server hosting a model
Decoupling token generation from the attention mechanism
Exporting model weights to an unauthorized open-source format

questions.explanation: Jailbreaking uses adversarial phrasing or hypothetical framing to elicit restricted content from aligned models.
questions.learnNote: Safety guardrails can be challenged by adversarial prompt formulations.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between top-p (nucleus) sampling and top-k sampling?

options.text: Top-p selects from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p; top-k selects from a fixed k highest-probability tokens
Top-p limits the context window size; top-k limits the total generation length
Top-p applies only to embeddings; top-k applies only to chat completions
Top-p is deterministic; top-k is completely random

questions.explanation: Top-p dynamic thresholding adapts the candidate pool based on probability distribution shape, whereas top-k fixes the candidate count.
questions.learnNote: Sampling algorithms control the candidate token pool using either cumulative probabilities or fixed counts.

questions.prompt: What is multi-turn conversation memory in an LLM application?

options.text: Maintaining relevant dialogue history across consecutive user and assistant messages
Permanently saving every user interaction into a central vector database
Fine-tuning the model weights after each chat interaction
Precomputing embeddings for all future user questions

questions.explanation: Conversation memory manages prior dialogue turns within the context window so the model understands contextual references.
questions.learnNote: Conversational applications must supply previous relevant exchanges to maintain context across messages.

questions.prompt: What is function calling (tool use) in an LLM API?

options.text: The model generating structured arguments to call external tools or APIs defined by the application
The model executing arbitrary Python code directly inside the API server
The application rewriting model weights during a live request
A protocol for streaming audio tokens across WebSockets

questions.explanation: Function calling allows models to detect when tools are needed and output structured JSON arguments for the client to execute.
questions.learnNote: Applications can declare callable functions that models invoke by producing structured inputs.

questions.prompt: Why set timeouts on model requests?

options.text: To bound how long an application waits
To guarantee every request succeeds
To eliminate rate limits
To remove the need for retries

questions.explanation: Timeouts bound waiting time and allow the application to recover or report failure.
questions.learnNote: External services can be slow or unavailable.

questions.prompt: What is an idempotent operation?

options.text: One that has the same intended effect when repeated
One that must always fail on retry
One that cannot be logged
One that requires a GPU

questions.explanation: Idempotency prevents repeated requests from creating duplicate effects.
questions.learnNote: Network retries can send the same operation more than once.

questions.prompt: How should an application handle model-generated tool arguments?

options.text: Validate and authorize them before executing the tool
Execute them without checks
Treat them as administrator instructions
Store them as secrets

questions.explanation: Model output is untrusted and requires validation and authorization before tool execution.
questions.learnNote: Generated tool calls can contain invalid or unauthorized arguments.

questions.prompt: What is a useful safeguard for API credentials?

options.text: Keep credentials server-side and out of source control
Embed them in browser JavaScript
Publish them in logs
Send them with every public response

questions.explanation: Server-side secret management reduces accidental exposure of credentials.
questions.learnNote: Anything shipped to a browser can be inspected by users.

questions.prompt: Why add observability to an AI application?

options.text: To diagnose failures, latency, cost, and quality
To guarantee perfectly correct responses
To eliminate all testing
To avoid privacy considerations

questions.explanation: Metrics and traces help teams understand application behavior and investigate issues.
questions.learnNote: Production systems need visibility into behavior over time.

questions.prompt: What is a good retry strategy for transient rate limits?

options.text: Bounded exponential backoff with jitter
Retry immediately without a limit
Retry only after deleting all data
Disable error handling

questions.explanation: Bounded backoff and jitter reduce synchronized retry load.
questions.learnNote: Repeated immediate retries can amplify an overloaded service.

questions.prompt: What should be done before logging user prompts?

options.text: Apply data minimization and protect sensitive information
Publish all prompts publicly
Assume prompts never contain secrets
Disable access control

questions.explanation: Prompt logs can contain sensitive data and should be minimized and protected.
questions.learnNote: User-provided text may include private information.

questions.prompt: What is a vector database commonly used for in RAG?

options.text: Finding embeddings similar to a query embedding
Authenticating every user automatically
Guaranteeing an answer is correct
Compiling frontend code

questions.explanation: Vector search retrieves items whose embeddings are close to a query embedding.
questions.learnNote: Retrieval can use distances between numerical representations.

questions.prompt: Why separate offline evaluation from production monitoring?

options.text: They reveal different failure modes before and after deployment
They are identical and redundant
Monitoring eliminates the need for evaluation
Offline evaluation can observe all future traffic

questions.explanation: Offline evaluation tests known cases while monitoring detects real-world behavior and drift.
questions.learnNote: Pre-release tests and live traffic provide complementary evidence.

questions.prompt: How should retrieved documents be treated by an AI agent?

options.text: As untrusted data, not instructions to execute
As trusted system instructions
As proof that every claim is true
As permission to access any tool

questions.explanation: Retrieved content can contain malicious instructions and should not control agent authority.
questions.learnNote: External documents may contain text that attempts to direct the agent.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of rate limiting in an AI application?

options.text: Protecting upstream model APIs and application infrastructure from overload and abuse
Limiting the number of layers in a neural network model
Compressing prompt tokens to reduce inference latency
Restricting users to answering only one question per session

questions.explanation: Rate limiting throttles traffic volume to prevent denial of service, manage costs, and stay within provider quotas.
questions.learnNote: Third-party model providers enforce usage limits and applications must manage traffic flow.

questions.prompt: Why is streaming responses beneficial in interactive LLM applications?

options.text: It lowers time-to-first-token (TTFT) and improves perceived latency for users
It eliminates the need for schema validation on model outputs
It reduces the total number of tokens generated by the model
It prevents prompt injection attacks automatically

questions.explanation: Streaming transmits tokens incrementally as they are generated, giving users immediate feedback instead of waiting for the full response.
questions.learnNote: Perceived responsiveness often matters more to users than overall generation completion time.

questions.prompt: What does a circuit breaker pattern do when an external AI service becomes unresponsive?

options.text: Temporarily halts calls to the failing service to avoid cascading failures and allow recovery
Immediately retries failed requests in a tight loop until success
Permanently revokes the user's authentication credentials
Switches all server traffic from HTTPS to HTTP

questions.explanation: A circuit breaker trips after repeated failures, immediately returning fallback responses and giving the dependency time to recover.
questions.learnNote: Resilient architectures avoid overwhelming degraded downstream dependencies.

questions.prompt: What is prompt drift in production AI systems?

options.text: Degradation or change in model behavior over time due to upstream updates or shifting input distributions
A network error where tokens arrive out of order
The physical movement of data between cloud regions
Gradual memory leaks in browser JavaScript

questions.explanation: Prompt drift occurs when changes to models, retrieval corpora, or user input distributions alter application behavior.
questions.learnNote: A prompt that worked reliably during testing may produce different outcomes over time as underlying systems evolve.

questions.prompt: What is the principle of least privilege when granting tools to an AI agent?

options.text: Granting the agent only the minimum tool capabilities and permissions necessary for its task
Allowing the agent unrestricted administrative access to simplify code
Preventing the agent from executing any external functions
Giving all agents identical global database credentials

questions.explanation: Least privilege minimizes potential damage if an agent is misled or compromised by untrusted instructions.
questions.learnNote: Limiting tool scopes reduces the blast radius of unexpected or hijacked model actions.

questions.prompt: What is semantic versioning of prompt templates?

options.text: Tracking changes to system and task prompts to manage behavior changes and rollback regressions
Converting prompt strings into semantic vector embeddings
Translating prompt templates into different human languages
Sorting prompt tokens alphabetically before transmission

questions.explanation: Version controlling prompts ensures reproducibility, allows A/B testing, and enables fast rollbacks when prompts degrade performance.
questions.learnNote: Prompt modifications can alter system behavior just as significantly as application code changes.

questions.prompt: Why should an AI application implement output guardrails?

options.text: To detect and filter policy violations, sensitive data leaks, or malformed responses before reaching users
To accelerate token generation speed from the model provider
To replace backend unit and integration test suites
To compress model responses into binary formats

questions.explanation: Output guardrails provide a defense-in-depth layer checking that generated outputs meet safety, privacy, and quality policies.
questions.learnNote: Even well-prompted models can occasionally produce unsafe, biased, or non-compliant responses.

questions.prompt: What is token usage tracking essential for in production AI applications?

options.text: Monitoring operational costs, enforcing user quotas, and detecting anomalous consumption
Preventing SQL injection attacks against application databases
Generating cryptographic keys for session authorization
Calculating model accuracy scores automatically

questions.explanation: Tracking input and output tokens provides visibility into per-user and per-feature costs, budget adherence, and anomalous usage patterns.
questions.learnNote: LLM provider billing is directly tied to token volumes across requests and responses.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of canary deployments for AI application updates?

options.text: Routing a small fraction of traffic to the new model or prompt to verify quality and safety before full rollout
Deploying model weights to user browser environments
Running automated tests exclusively on synthetic datasets
Encrypting network connections between microservices

questions.explanation: Canary releases expose updates to limited live traffic, reducing the impact of unexpected behavioral shifts or regressions.
questions.learnNote: Gradually exposing a new model configuration helps detect unexpected real-world degradation early.

questions.prompt: How should an AI system handle sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in prompts?

options.text: Redact or mask PII before sending text to external model APIs and logs
Include PII in the system instruction to improve contextual personalization
Store PII permanently in public vector database indices
Base64-encode PII and append it to prompt URLs

questions.explanation: Redacting or anonymizing PII before external transmission minimizes privacy compliance risks and prevents accidental exposure.
questions.learnNote: Transmitting personal information to external providers requires strict privacy and compliance safeguards.

questions.prompt: What is the primary objective of RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)?

options.text: Aligning model behavior with human intent, preferences, and safety criteria
Increasing the raw token generation speed of the model
Eliminating the need for a pretraining phase
Compressing model parameters to fit on consumer hardware

questions.explanation: RLHF uses human preference comparisons to fine-tune a model via reward modeling and reinforcement learning toward helpful and safe outputs.
questions.learnNote: Pretrained models optimize for next-token prediction, which does not inherently prioritize human values or safety.

questions.prompt: What is red teaming in the context of AI models?

options.text: Adversarial testing designed to discover vulnerabilities, harmful behaviors, and policy violations
Collaborative pair programming between model developers
Benchmarking GPU clock speeds under extreme temperatures
Automating customer support ticket categorization

questions.explanation: Red teaming actively probes models with edge cases and adversarial inputs to uncover failure modes before deployment.
questions.learnNote: Security and safety evaluations often use adversarial testing to find vulnerabilities that standard benchmarks miss.

questions.prompt: What is sycophancy in large language models?

options.text: The tendency of a model to agree with a user's stated opinion even when it is factually incorrect
A hardware fault causing repetitive token generation
The ability of a model to translate between ancient languages
A security attack that steals model weights via side channels

questions.explanation: Sycophancy occurs when models tailor responses to validate user biases or beliefs rather than remaining truthful.
questions.learnNote: Preference training can inadvertently reward agreeable responses over truthful ones.

questions.prompt: What is Constitutional AI as pioneered in model alignment?

options.text: Using a set of written principles to guide self-critique and revision during training
Requiring government approval before training any frontier model
Hardcoding ethical rules into model GPU firmware
Restricting model training to open-source legal documents

questions.explanation: Constitutional AI specifies high-level principles that the model uses to evaluate and refine its own outputs with minimal human feedback.
questions.learnNote: Alignment can leverage AI feedback governed by explicit behavioral principles.

questions.prompt: What is a model card used for?

options.text: Documenting model architecture, intended use cases, limitations, and evaluation performance
Purchasing inference API compute credits from cloud providers
A physical smart card containing encrypted model weights
A software license agreement for open-weights distribution

questions.explanation: Model cards provide standardized documentation on intended tasks, benchmark results, out-of-scope uses, and known ethical considerations.
questions.learnNote: Responsible deployment relies on transparent documentation of system boundaries and test results.

questions.prompt: What does alignment tax refer to in AI development?

options.text: A potential drop in performance or capabilities on certain benchmarks caused by safety interventions
Government tariffs imposed on imported AI compute chips
The financial cost of paying human annotators for dataset labeling
Cloud hosting fees incurred during safety evaluations

questions.explanation: The alignment tax describes any degradation in general capability or fluency that results from imposing safety and behavioral constraints.
questions.learnNote: Constraining model outputs to safe distributions can sometimes affect performance on unconstrained tasks.

questions.prompt: What is watermarking in generative AI outputs?

options.text: Embedding subtle, detectable statistical patterns into generated text or media to identify synthetic origin
Printing a visible copyright logo across generated images
Erasing copyrighted material from training datasets
Restricting model API access to verified corporate domains

questions.explanation: Watermarking alters token selection or media features slightly so automated detectors can identify AI-generated content without degrading quality.
questions.learnNote: Detecting synthetic media often relies on signals embedded directly into the generation process.

questions.prompt: What is algorithmic bias in machine learning systems?

options.text: Systematic and unfair discrimination in predictions resulting from biased data or flawed assumptions
Random measurement noise that cancels out over time
The deliberate preference for faster algorithms over slower ones
A hardware clock skew between distributed training servers

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias reflects historical inequities, unrepresentative sampling, or proxy variables in training data that lead to unfair outcomes.
questions.learnNote: Models trained on historical data often reproduce or amplify existing disparities.

questions.prompt: What is the goal of mechanistic interpretability?

options.text: Reverse-engineering neural networks to understand the internal circuits and representations driving decisions
Measuring physical energy consumption of server fans during training
Replacing neural networks with handwritten decision trees
Converting Python model scripts into machine assembly code

questions.explanation: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural network weights and activations form functional circuits that compute specific features.
questions.learnNote: Understanding black-box model internals helps verify safety before deployment.

questions.prompt: What is reward hacking in reinforcement learning systems?

options.text: When an agent exploits loopholes in a reward specification to achieve a high score without fulfilling the intended goal
An unauthorized cyberattack modifying database reward values
Paying users cryptocurrency to submit feedback on model outputs
Overfitting on the training set due to too many training epochs

questions.explanation: Reward hacking occurs when an optimizer finds degenerate shortcuts that maximize the formal reward metric while violating designers' actual intent.
questions.learnNote: Optimizing a proxy metric can produce unexpected behaviors that diverge from the true objective.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind the ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) prompting framework?

options.text: Interleaving thought generation with action execution and observation retrieval in a loop
Compiling Python model logic into React JavaScript components
Using reactive streams to deliver tokens to web browsers
Executing all available tools simultaneously without reasoning

questions.explanation: ReAct prompts the model to generate reasoning traces ('Thoughts') followed by tool actions ('Actions') and environment feedback ('Observations').
questions.learnNote: Autonomous agents alternate between deliberating on the next step and interacting with external tools.

questions.prompt: Why is a maximum recursion or step limit essential for autonomous agents?

options.text: To prevent infinite execution loops and unbounded compute costs when an agent cannot resolve a task
To ensure that agent memory fits inside CPU L1 cache
To comply with international data transfer regulations
To prevent the agent from outputting markdown formatting

questions.explanation: A step limit guarantees that an agent trapped in a repetitive failure loop will terminate predictably rather than running indefinitely.
questions.learnNote: Multi-step agent loops require safeguards against unconstrained execution.

questions.prompt: What is the role of reflection or self-critique in agent architectures?

options.text: Evaluating past actions and intermediate outputs to identify errors and adjust subsequent plans
Inverting model tensor dimensions during inference
Mirroring database transactions across backup availability zones
Translating agent logs into human speech

questions.explanation: Self-reflection allows an agent to assess its trajectory, diagnose why an approach failed, and formulate a corrected plan.
questions.learnNote: Agents can improve task completion rates by critically evaluating their own intermediate results.

questions.prompt: What is a plan-and-solve agent architecture?

options.text: Decomposing a complex task into sequential sub-tasks before executing them individually
Executing actions purely at random until a goal test passes
Generating multiple answers and choosing the shortest string
Replacing external tools with hardcoded database queries

questions.explanation: Plan-and-solve architectures separate high-level strategy (planning) from low-level execution, reducing drift during multi-step tasks.
questions.learnNote: Separating roadmap generation from execution helps agents tackle complex multi-stage objectives.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes short-term memory from long-term memory in an AI agent?

options.text: Short-term memory lives in the current context window; long-term memory is persisted externally for retrieval
Short-term memory stores numbers; long-term memory stores text
Short-term memory uses GPUs; long-term memory uses TPUs
Short-term memory is permanent; long-term memory expires after each turn

questions.explanation: Short-term memory holds active conversation and scratchpad state, while long-term memory uses vector databases or files across sessions.
questions.learnNote: Agents combine working context with external persistence to maintain knowledge across extended tasks.

questions.prompt: What is human-in-the-loop (HITL) authorization in agentic workflows?

options.text: Requiring human confirmation before an agent executes high-impact or irreversible actions
Having human annotators write every model prompt by hand
Running all model inference on user client machines
Requiring human approval to load static webpage assets

questions.explanation: HITL gates critical operations (such as making financial transactions or deleting databases) on explicit user verification.
questions.learnNote: High-stakes tool executions often require human oversight before proceeding.

questions.prompt: What is a subagent in hierarchical agent systems?

options.text: A specialized agent spawned by a supervisor to complete a delegated subtask and report back
A downgraded model used when network bandwidth is constrained
A client-side JavaScript worker handling DOM rendering
An automated script that restarts crashed server instances

questions.explanation: Hierarchical architectures use a coordinator agent that delegates focused sub-problems to dedicated subagents with specific toolsets.
questions.learnNote: Decomposing large problems into specialized workers keeps individual contexts focused and manageable.

questions.prompt: How should an agent handle a tool execution error?

options.text: Feed the error message back into the model context so it can adapt its parameters or try an alternative
Immediately crash the entire server application without logging
Fabricate a successful response and continue execution
Disable all tools permanently for the remainder of the session

questions.explanation: Exposing structured error messages in the observation turn enables agents to self-correct typos, invalid parameters, or unexpected states.
questions.learnNote: Tool failure details provide essential feedback for an agent to diagnose and recover.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of dynamic few-shot example selection for tool-using agents?

options.text: Selecting the most relevant tool usage demonstrations based on the current user query to save context
Hardcoding every possible tool example into the system prompt
Fine-tuning the model tokenizer on tool documentation
Randomly rotating examples to introduce unpredictability

questions.explanation: Dynamic selection retrieves only relevant examples via vector similarity, avoiding context bloat from extensive tool libraries.
questions.learnNote: When tool libraries are large, context space can be preserved by injecting only relevant demonstrations.

questions.prompt: What is context stuffing in agent loops and why is it problematic?

options.text: Accumulating unfiltered tool outputs in the context until token limits are exhausted or reasoning degrades
Adding too many model parameters to a deep learning network
Packing multiple GPU cards into a single server rack
Submitting multiple form inputs simultaneously in a browser

questions.explanation: Bloating context with noisy tool responses increases cost, raises latency, and causes the model to lose track of the core objective.
questions.learnNote: Unbounded accumulation of intermediate tool logs can overwhelm model attention.

questions.prompt: What is a Vision-Language Model (VLM)?

options.text: A model capable of processing and reasoning over both text and image inputs simultaneously
A model that only generates computer code for graphic shaders
A traditional optical character recognition (OCR) engine without a language model
A hardware display driver optimized for machine learning

questions.explanation: VLMs integrate visual encoders with language models to understand, analyze, and answer questions about images and text jointly.
questions.learnNote: Multimodal systems combine representations from different sensory modalities into a shared reasoning space.

questions.prompt: What is CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) primarily trained to do?

options.text: Learn a shared embedding space where matching text and image pairs have high cosine similarity
Directly generate photorealistic 3D animations from audio
Compress video files into MP4 format using neural codecs
Translate spoken audio directly into foreign subtitles

questions.explanation: CLIP uses contrastive learning across massive image-text pairs so visual concepts and natural language descriptions map to nearby vectors.
questions.learnNote: Cross-modal retrieval relies on embedding visual and textual concepts into a common coordinate system.

questions.prompt: What is visual prompting in modern vision models?

options.text: Guiding the model's visual attention by drawing bounding boxes, arrows, or circles directly on the input image
Generating video clips from command-line terminal commands
Displaying a popup window asking users to upload images
Formatting image metadata into XML tags

questions.explanation: Visual prompting overlays visual markers (like colored circles or boxes) on images to direct model focus toward specific regions.
questions.learnNote: Directing model attention can be achieved through visual cues applied directly to input media.

questions.prompt: How do Vision Transformers (ViT) process images?

options.text: By splitting an image into fixed-size patches, flattening them, and treating them as a sequence of tokens
By converting images into ASCII text characters before convolution
By scanning pixels one at a time from top to bottom
By training a separate convolutional network for every color channel

questions.explanation: ViT breaks images into a grid of patches (e.g., 16x16 pixels) and applies standard self-attention mechanisms identical to text transformers.
questions.learnNote: Transformer attention mechanisms can process visual patches analogously to text tokens.

questions.prompt: What is automatic speech recognition (ASR)?

options.text: Converting spoken acoustic audio signals into readable text transcripts
Synthesizing artificial human speech from written paragraphs
Compressing MP3 audio files to reduce disk footprint
Filtering background hiss from audio recordings

questions.explanation: ASR systems (such as Whisper) transcribe spoken language audio into written text.
questions.learnNote: Speech-to-text systems map audio waveforms into sequences of linguistic tokens.

questions.prompt: What is text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis?

options.text: Generating spoken natural audio waveforms from input text
Translating foreign subtitles into English text
Detecting speaker gender and sentiment from audio files
Transcribing microphone recordings into markdown files

questions.explanation: TTS models convert written sentences into natural, expressive human-like spoken audio.
questions.learnNote: Generating audible voice output from written language is a core multimodal capability.

questions.prompt: How do latent diffusion models generate images from text descriptions?

options.text: By iteratively removing noise from a latent representation guided by text embeddings
By stitching together pre-existing stock photographs from a database
By rendering vector graphics using mathematical bezier curves
By executing Python turtle graphics commands

questions.explanation: Diffusion models start from random Gaussian noise in a compressed latent space and iteratively denoise it conditioned on prompt embeddings.
questions.learnNote: Generative image models often work by gradually reversing a noise-adding process conditioned on text.

questions.prompt: What is spatial reasoning in vision-language models?

options.text: The ability to understand relative physical positions, orientations, and distances between objects in an image
The amount of hard drive storage required to store image files
The rate at which satellite imagery is downloaded from orbit
The process of calculating server rack space in a datacenter

questions.explanation: Spatial reasoning enables models to answer queries about which objects are above, behind, closer, or larger than others.
questions.learnNote: Multimodal models must learn physical geometric relationships depicted within 2D image projections.

questions.prompt: What is image tokenization in multimodal architectures?

options.text: Converting visual regions or patches into discrete or continuous vector representations compatible with transformer layers
Watermarking images with a cryptographic token to prevent forgery
Minting non-fungible digital tokens (NFTs) from user graphics
Compressing JPEG images into smaller byte arrays

questions.explanation: Image tokenization transforms visual data into representations that can be concatenated with text tokens in a unified model.
questions.learnNote: Integrating vision and language requires converting continuous visual information into tokens the model can attend to.

questions.prompt: What is document visual question answering (DocVQA)?

options.text: Extracting and reasoning over information from complex documents featuring tables, forms, and layout formatting
Automatically converting PDF documents into plain text files
Checking spelling errors in word processing applications
Validating digital cryptographic signatures on legal agreements

questions.explanation: DocVQA models understand both typographic content and visual spatial layout (tables, headers, forms, diagrams) to answer queries.
questions.learnNote: Document understanding requires interpreting visual layout cues alongside textual content.
